title: Tighten Trade-Support Penalty

findings.title: No regression test for the exponent shape
findings.description: The entire purpose of this change is to make the graduated penalty curve steeper (2 -> 3). However, no test asserts the specific shape. The only test that exercises the graduated zone is `test_graduated_between_floor_and_support` in tests/unit/test_phase2_support.py, which only checks `0 <= pen <= SUPPORT_PENALTY_MAX` — that assertion would pass for ANY exponent >= 1 (or even 0.5, 0.1, etc.). A future accidental change of TRADE_SUPPORT_PENALTY_EXPONENT to 2.0, 4.0, or even 0.5 would not be caught by the test suite.
findings.suggestion: Add a single test that pins the expected penalty value for a known (executed, min_support, pool_floor, exponent) tuple, e.g. with min_support=120, pool_floor=40, executed=80, exponent=3.0: shortfall=40/120=0.333, penalty=0.333**3 * 5.0 ~= 0.185. Also assert a monkey-patched exponent change (e.g. set to 2.0) yields the quadratic value. This locks down the shape and the config wiring in one test.

findings.title: Dead cap code in numba penalty
findings.description: The numba `_batch_static_penalties_numba` contains `if val > penalty_max: out[i] = penalty_max` after `val = shortfall ** exponent * penalty_max`. With exponent >= 1 and shortfall in (0,1), val is strictly less than penalty_max, so the cap is dead code. This was also dead with exponent=2 (pre-existing) — not introduced by this change, just made more obviously dead. Similarly the Python versions' `min(..., _cfg.SUPPORT_PENALTY_MAX)` cap is now dead in the graduated zone. Harmless, but could be removed for clarity in a follow-up.

findings.title: Minor inconsistency: divisor guard differs between numba and Python
findings.description: _static_support_penalty (Python) uses `max(support_target, 1)` as divisor; _static_penalty_py (Python) uses `_cfg.MIN_TRADE_SUPPORT` directly; _batch_static_penalties_numba uses `min_support` directly. If `min_support == 0` is ever passed, the two Python versions and the numba version diverge (one raises ZeroDivisionError, the two others too). Pre-existing inconsistency, not introduced by this change, and the config default is 120 so it never fires in practice.

edge_cases.executed_eq_min_support: returns 0.0 in all 3 sites; exponent irrelevant
edge_cases.executed_lt_pool_floor: returns 2.0 * penalty_max in all 3 sites; exponent irrelevant (hard reject)
edge_cases.shortfall_in_0_1: val = shortfall**3 * penalty_max in (0, penalty_max); cap is dead but harmless
edge_cases.shortfall_eq_0: guarded by executed >= min_support check, never reaches the power
edge_cases.shortfall_eq_1: guarded by executed < pool_floor check, never reaches the power

security.concerns: None — config-driven numeric exponent, no external input

test_adequacy.concerns: Existing test suite does not pin the exponent shape; see F1.

verdict_rationale: Implementation is correct, minimal (+10/-4), and well-scoped. All three penalty sites consistently use TRADE_SUPPORT_PENALTY_EXPONENT (3.0). Edge cases (zero, below-floor) are correctly guarded. No security concerns. The only meaningful gap is the lack of a regression test that pins the specific exponent value (F1, low-severity). The two info-level findings (F2 dead cap, F3 divisor inconsistency) are pre-existing and not introduced by this change. Approving with the suggestion to add a shape-pinning test as a follow-up.
notes: Single clean commit; no stray Task-1 commit
Numba signature change (added exponent param) will trigger JIT recompile; @njit(cache=True) handles this correctly
Hard-floor penalty (2.0 * SUPPORT_PENALTY_MAX for executed < pool_floor) correctly left unchanged — it is not in the graduated zone
float() cast in Python paths is a sensible type-safety measure for the numba call
